failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM606 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch and Guide Wear - All variants
items.whatHappens: The duplex timing chain and plastic guide rails can stretch and wear over high mileage, leading to a distinct rattling noise on cold starts. If ignored, the chain can jump a tooth, causing valve-to-piston contact and catastrophic engine failure.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, a timing chain and guide kit replacement is straightforward and cost-effective. If the engine has already suffered valve damage, a full reconditioned unit is the only viable path.

items.title: Injector Seal Weeping ("Black Death") - All variants
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the injectors degrade over time, allowing combustion gases to escape. This creates a black, crusty carbon buildup around the injector heads and can lead to difficult cold starts or rough idling.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the seals and cleaning the cylinder head is inexpensive and should be done preventatively.

items.title: Head Gasket Failure - .960 and .962 turbocharged variants
items.whatHappens: The turbocharged OM606 variants generate significantly higher cylinder pressures and heat. Over time, the head gasket can fail, leading to coolant loss, overheating, and combustion gases entering the cooling system.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught before the cylinder head warps, a head gasket replacement is viable. If the head has warped or the block is damaged, a full reconditioned or rebuilt unit is required.

failures.goodYearsLine: The OM606 is widely regarded as one of Mercedes’ most robust inline-6 diesels, offering a significant refinement and power step up from the OM603 it succeeded. Units maintained with regular oil changes routinely exceed 300,000 miles without major internal issues .

variants.title: OM606 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: The OM606 family shares the same fundamental 3.0L inline-6 block and pre-chamber head design, but forced induction and tuning vary depending on the chassis. Identifying your exact sub-code ensures you order the correct injection pump, turbo, and ancillary components. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (E 300 D), S-Class W140 (S 300), G-Class W463 (G 300 GD) - Key technical difference: The base naturally aspirated variant, featuring a simpler ancillary layout without turbo plumbing and a mechanical Bosch PES injection pump calibrated for lower output. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; no unique widespread defects beyond standard high-mileage wear. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the turbo variants; the injection pump, exhaust manifold, and oil return lines differ significantly. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (E 300 TD), S-Class W140 (S 350 TD), G-Class W463 (G 350 TD) - Key technical difference: Adds a turbocharger and intercooler to the 3.0L block, requiring a higher-capacity mechanical injection pump, revised piston cooling jets, and an upgraded cooling system to handle the additional heat. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; turbocharger shaft wear and head gasket failure under boost are the primary additional wear items. - Interchange note: Can be swapped with the .910 block, but requires the complete turbo kit, different injection pump, and revised engine management linkages. - Fitted to: S-Class W140 (late S 350 TD), G-Class W463/W461 (late G 350 TD) - Key technical difference: A later revision of the turbocharged architecture, featuring updated emissions calibration, revised vacuum pump orientation, and specific accessory brackets for the later W140 and W461 commercial/military chassis. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; vacuum pump leaks are slightly more prevalent on this specific revision due to the revised mounting angle. - Interchange note: Directly interchangeable with the .960 in most passenger car applications, provided the injection pump and vacuum pump are swapped to match the original chassis specification.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM606 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used OM606 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and a recent timing chain guide inspection. Given the age of these vehicles, the primary risk is hidden corrosion or degraded rubber seals, so a compression test is mandatory before purchase.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM606 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will address the common failure points by fitting a new timing chain guide kit, updated injector seals, and a refreshed mechanical injection pump, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM606 engine rebuild is justified for high-mileage G-Class applications or classic W140 restorations where originality and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM606 engine is installed by specialists familiar with classic Mercedes mechanical diesels, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM606 is typically found in vehicles valued between £2,000 and £10,000 for standard examples (though classic low-mileage W140 and G-Class models can command much higher premiums), a full replacement can represent a significant portion of the car's worth. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.question: How much does a Mercedes OM606 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes OM606 engine typically costs between £1,800 and £2,800 for supply only . Fitted costs generally range from £2,700 to £4,000 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £600 but carry higher risk due to the engine's age. items.question: What is the most common failure on the OM606 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are timing chain stretch and plastic guide rail wear, alongside injector seal weeping ("Black Death") and head gasket failure on the turbocharged .960 and .962 variants. Timing chain rattle on cold starts is the primary warning sign, which can lead to catastrophic valve damage if ignored, whereas injector seal failure causes black carbon buildup but is a cheap and routine fix. Get quotes for a rebuilt OM606 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the OM606 engine?
items.answer: The OM606 was fitted to the W124 E-Class (E 300 D, E 300 TD), the W140 S-Class (S 300, S 350 TD), and the W463/W461 G-Class (G 300 GD, G 350 TD), serving as the definitive 6-cylinder diesel for these premium and off-road chassis throughout the 1990s. Check your registration to confirm your exact OM606 fitment

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned OM606 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned OM606 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the age of these vehicles. A proper rebuild will replace the timing chain, plastic guide rails, tensioner, and injector seals, eliminating the most common failure points, whereas used engines may appear cheaper upfront but often hide stretched chains that will fail shortly after installation. Compare reconditioned OM606 engine prices from UK specialists

items.question: What is the difference between OM606.910, .960, and .962?
items.answer: The OM606.910 is the 3.0L naturally aspirated variant, the OM606.960 is the 3.0L turbocharged version requiring a higher-capacity mechanical injection pump and upgraded cooling, and the OM606.962 is a later turbocharged revision with updated emissions calibration and revised vacuum pump orientation for later W140 and W461 chassis.
